questions.question: What is JUnit 5 and how do you write a basic test?
questions.title: JUnit 5 Basics Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **JUnit 5** is the standard testing framework for Java, made of three modules: **JUnit Platform** (the launcher that runs tests), **JUnit Jupiter** (the modern API with `@Test` and `Assertions`), and **JUnit Vintage** (runs old JUnit 4 tests). A basic test is a method annotated with `@Test` that arranges inputs, calls the code, and verifies the result with a static assertion like `assertEquals`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write a JUnit 5 test from scratch and know the Jupiter API is what you actually import
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing JUnit 4 imports (org.junit.Test) with JUnit 5, or marking the test method public/returning a value out of habit
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the three modules and explain that Jupiter is the API you write against while the Platform launches it

sections.title: What JUnit 5 Is
sections.content:
**JUnit 5** is the de-facto unit-testing framework for the JVM and the default in Spring Boot. Unlike JUnit 4's single jar, JUnit 5 is **modular**: **JUnit Platform** is the foundation that discovers and launches tests (IDEs and Maven build on it); **JUnit Jupiter** is the new programming model — the `@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, and `Assertions` you write against; and **JUnit Vintage** is a bridge that runs legacy JUnit 3/4 tests on the new platform.

A test is just a method annotated with `@Test`. In JUnit 5 the class and methods can be package-private (no `public` needed), and a test method returns `void`.

sections.title: The Three Modules
sections.content:
blue|JUnit Platform|~Launches & discovers tests|IDEs/Maven build on it|TestEngine API|the foundation layer
emerald|JUnit Jupiter|~The API you write|@Test, @BeforeEach|Assertions, Assumptions|new programming model
amber|JUnit Vintage|~Runs JUnit 3/4 tests|backward compatibility|migrate gradually|drop once migrated

sections.title: Anatomy of a Basic Test
sections.content:
A clean JUnit 5 test follows three labelled steps:

| Step | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Arrange** | Build inputs and the object under test | `var calc = new Calculator();` |
| **Act** | Call the method being tested | `int sum = calc.add(2, 3);` |
| **Assert** | Verify the observable result | `assertEquals(5, sum);` |

sections.title: Your First JUnit 5 Test
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrong import.** Importing `org.junit.Test` (JUnit 4) instead of `org.junit.jupiter.api.Test` — the test silently won't run under JUnit 5.
- **Making everything public.** JUnit 5 doesn't require `public` on classes or test methods; the habit is harmless but unnecessary.
- **Returning a value.** Test methods must return `void`.
- **No assertion.** A method with `@Test` but no assertion passes trivially and proves nothing.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three modules** — Platform (launcher), Jupiter (the API), Vintage (runs JUnit 4).
- **`@Test`** comes from `org.junit.jupiter.api.Test`.
- **No `public` needed** — package-private classes and methods work.
- **Static assertions** — `import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*`.
- **AAA structure** — Arrange, Act, Assert for readability.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JUnit 5 is the standard unit-testing framework for Java, and it's what Spring Boot uses by default. The thing that's different from JUnit 4 is that it's modular — it's actually three pieces. The first is the JUnit Platform, which is the foundation that discovers and launches tests; that's what your IDE and Maven hook into. The second is JUnit Jupiter, which is the API I actually write against — the Test annotation, the lifecycle annotations, and the Assertions class. The third is JUnit Vintage, which is a bridge that lets old JUnit 4 tests run on the new platform, so a team can migrate gradually.

Writing a basic test is simple. I create a class, and inside it a method annotated with Test. In JUnit 5 I don't need to make the class or the method public — package-private is fine. Inside the method I follow Arrange, Act, Assert: I build my inputs and the object under test, I call the method I'm testing, and then I verify the result with a static assertion like assertEquals, passing the expected value first, then the actual.

The one gotcha I'd call out is the import. The Test annotation has to come from org dot junit dot jupiter dot api. If you accidentally import the JUnit 4 Test annotation from org dot junit, the test just won't be picked up. To stand out, I'd name the three modules and explain that Jupiter is the API I write while the Platform is what runs it.

questions.question: What are the most important JUnit 5 annotations?
questions.title: JUnit 5 Annotations | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: The core JUnit 5 annotations are **`@Test`** (marks a test), the lifecycle hooks **`@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach`** (run around every test) and **`@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll`** (run once per class, must be `static`), plus **`@DisplayName`** (readable report name), **`@Disabled`** (skip with a reason), and **`@Nested`** (group related tests). They come from `org.junit.jupiter.api`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know each annotation's timing — especially that @BeforeAll/@AfterAll are static and per-class
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting @BeforeAll must be static, or confusing @BeforeEach (every test) with @BeforeAll (once)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @BeforeAll is static because by default JUnit creates a fresh test instance per method

sections.title: The Annotations You Use Daily
sections.content: JUnit 5's everyday annotations all live in `org.junit.jupiter.api`. **`@Test`** marks a method as a test. The **lifecycle** annotations control setup and teardown: **`@BeforeEach`** runs before *every* test to create fresh state; **`@AfterEach`** cleans up after every test; **`@BeforeAll`** and **`@AfterAll`** run *once* for the whole class and must be `static` by default. Reporting and control annotations include **`@DisplayName`** for human-readable names, **`@Disabled`** to skip a test (always with a reason), and **`@Nested`** to group related scenarios.

sections.title: Annotations at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|@Test|~Marks a test method|returns void|no public needed|the foundation
blue|@BeforeEach / @AfterEach|~Run around every test|fresh state per test|setup / cleanup|not static
amber|@BeforeAll / @AfterAll|~Run once per class|MUST be static|expensive shared setup|e.g. open a pool
violet|@DisplayName / @Disabled / @Nested|~Readability & control|readable report names|skip with a reason|group scenarios

sections.title: Lifecycle Annotations in Action
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`@BeforeAll` not static.** By default JUnit creates a new test instance per method, so a once-per-class hook must be `static` (unless you use `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`).
- **Confusing Each vs All.** `@BeforeEach` runs before every test; `@BeforeAll` runs once. Putting expensive setup in `@BeforeEach` slows the suite.
- **`@Disabled` with no reason.** Always pass a reason string so the skip is explained in reports.
- **JUnit 4 names.** It's `@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach`, not JUnit 4's `@Before`/`@After`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Test`** — marks a test; returns void.
- **`@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach`** — run around every test for fresh state.
- **`@BeforeAll`/`@AfterAll`** — run once per class; must be `static`.
- **`@DisplayName`** — readable name in reports and IDEs.
- **`@Disabled("reason")` and `@Nested`** — skip with context, group scenarios.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The annotations I reach for every day all come from the Jupiter API. The most basic is Test, which marks a method as a test. Then there are the lifecycle annotations. BeforeEach runs before every single test, and I use it to create fresh state so tests stay independent. AfterEach runs after every test to clean up. BeforeAll and AfterAll run just once for the whole class — BeforeAll for expensive setup like opening a connection pool, and AfterAll to tear it down. The important detail is that BeforeAll and AfterAll have to be static by default.

The reason they're static is that JUnit, by default, creates a brand new instance of the test class for each test method, so it can keep tests isolated. Because a once-per-class method can't belong to any single instance, it lives at the class level, which means static. If I really want them non-static, I can switch the class to the per-class lifecycle with the TestInstance annotation.

Beyond those, there are a few I use for readability and control. DisplayName gives a test a human-readable name that shows up in reports instead of the method name. Disabled skips a test, and I always pass a reason string so it's clear why. And Nested lets me group related tests into inner classes so the report reads like an outline.

The common mistake is forgetting BeforeAll must be static, or confusing BeforeEach with BeforeAll and putting heavy setup in the wrong one. To stand out, I'd explain that static requirement comes from JUnit's fresh-instance-per-test design.

questions.question: How do you use assertions in JUnit 5?
questions.title: JUnit 5 Assertions | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: JUnit 5 assertions are static methods on `org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions`: **`assertEquals(expected, actual)`** for value equality (expected first!), **`assertTrue`/`assertFalse`**, **`assertNull`/`assertNotNull`**, **`assertThrows`** to verify an exception, **`assertAll`** to group assertions, and **`assertSame`** for reference identity. Most teams layer **AssertJ**'s fluent `assertThat(x).isEqualTo(y)` on top for readability.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the core assertions, the expected-first parameter order, and how to test exceptions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Swapping expected and actual (which produces a backwards failure message) or using try/catch instead of assertThrows
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention assertThrows returns the exception so you can assert on its message, and assertAll reports all failures

sections.title: How Assertions Work
sections.content:
An **assertion** checks a condition and fails the test if it's false. In JUnit 5 they're static methods on **`Assertions`**, usually imported statically. The workhorse is **`assertEquals(expected, actual)`** — note the **expected value comes first**, so failure messages read "expected X but was Y." Other staples: **`assertTrue`/`assertFalse`** for booleans, **`assertNull`/`assertNotNull`**, **`assertThrows`** for exceptions, **`assertAll`** to run several assertions and report every failure, and **`assertSame`/`assertNotSame`** for reference identity.

Many teams add **AssertJ** for a fluent, readable style: `assertThat(price).isEqualTo(90.0)`.

sections.title: Assertion Toolbox
sections.content:
emerald|Value checks|~Compare results|assertEquals(expected, actual)|assertTrue / assertFalse|assertNull / assertNotNull
blue|Exception checks|~Verify failures|assertThrows(Type.class, ...)|returns the exception|assert on its message
amber|Grouping|~See all failures|assertAll(...)|runs every assertion|no stop at first
violet|Identity|~Same object?|assertSame / assertNotSame|reference, not value|rarely needed

sections.title: Core Assertions, Including Exceptions
Common Assertions Reference
sections.content:
| Assertion | Checks | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `assertEquals(exp, act)` | Value equality (uses `equals`) | `assertEquals(5, sum)` |
| `assertTrue(cond)` | Boolean is true | `assertTrue(list.isEmpty())` |
| `assertNull(obj)` | Reference is null | `assertNull(repo.find(0))` |
| `assertThrows(T, exec)` | Code throws `T`; returns it | `assertThrows(IAE.class, ...)` |
| `assertAll(...)` | Runs all, reports every failure | grouped field checks |
| `assertSame(a, b)` | Same object reference (`==`) | cached instance returned |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expected/actual swapped.** `assertEquals(actual, expected)` flips the message to "expected <yours> but was <correct>", which misleads during debugging.
- **try/catch for exceptions.** Wrapping in try/catch and calling `fail()` is verbose and error-prone; use `assertThrows`.
- **`assertEquals` on objects with no `equals()`.** It falls back to reference identity and fails unexpectedly — override `equals` or compare fields.
- **Multiple asserts that stop early.** Separate `assertEquals` calls stop at the first failure; `assertAll` shows all.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Expected first** — `assertEquals(expected, actual)` for correct messages.
- **`assertThrows` returns the exception** — assert on its message or cause.
- **`assertAll`** — groups assertions and reports every failure at once.
- **`assertSame` vs `assertEquals`** — identity (`==`) vs value (`equals`).
- **AssertJ** — `assertThat(x).isEqualTo(y)` reads better for complex checks.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
In JUnit 5, assertions are static methods on the Assertions class, and I usually import them statically so I can just call assertEquals directly. The one I use most is assertEquals, and the important detail is that the expected value comes first and the actual value second. That ordering matters because the failure message reads expected this but was that — if you swap them, the message is backwards and misleads you while debugging.

Beyond assertEquals, there's assertTrue and assertFalse for booleans, assertNull and assertNotNull for references, and assertThrows for exceptions. assertThrows is really useful because it doesn't just check that an exception was thrown — it returns the exception object, so I can then assert on its message or its cause. That's much cleaner than the old try-catch-then-fail pattern.

There's also assertAll, which lets me group several assertions together. Normally separate assertions stop at the first failure, but assertAll runs all of them and reports every failure at once, which is handy when I'm checking several fields of one object. And there's assertSame, which checks reference identity with double-equals rather than value equality — I rarely need it.

One gotcha is calling assertEquals on objects that don't override equals — it falls back to reference comparison and fails even when the values match. In practice a lot of teams add AssertJ on top, so you write assertThat(price).isEqualTo(ninety), which reads more naturally for complex objects and collections. To stand out, I'd mention that assertThrows returns the exception and assertAll surfaces all failures.

questions.question: What is a parameterized test in JUnit 5 and how do you write one?
questions.title: JUnit 5 Parameterized Tests | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **parameterized test** runs the *same* test logic against many inputs, so you write one method instead of copy-pasting. You mark it with **`@ParameterizedTest`** (not `@Test`) and supply data via a source: **`@ValueSource`** for a single array of literals, **`@CsvSource`** for input→expected rows, **`@MethodSource`** for complex objects, plus `@EnumSource` and `@NullSource`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can remove duplicate near-identical tests and pick the right argument source
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Test instead of @ParameterizedTest, or reaching for @MethodSource when @CsvSource is simpler
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Match the source to the data: @ValueSource for one arg, @CsvSource for pairs, @MethodSource for objects/null

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ParameterizedTest`** replaces `@Test` for data-driven tests.
- **`@ValueSource`** — one literal argument per run.
- **`@CsvSource`** — input→expected rows, with auto type conversion.
- **`@MethodSource`** — `static Stream<Arguments>` for objects/null.
- **`name`** attribute customizes each invocation's report label.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A parameterized test lets me run the same test logic against many different inputs, so instead of copy-pasting five almost-identical tests I write one. The key difference is that I annotate the method with ParameterizedTest instead of Test, and then I attach a source that supplies the data.

There are a few sources, and I pick based on the shape of my data. ValueSource is the simplest — it feeds a single array of literals, like a set of integers or strings, and the method takes one parameter. CsvSource is what I use for input and expected pairs; each row is comma-separated, so I can write something like the password abcd1234 maps to valid true, and JUnit even converts the types automatically. MethodSource is for when the arguments are complex objects or include nulls — I point it at a static factory method that returns a Stream of Arguments, and each Arguments dot of call becomes one test run. There are also EnumSource and NullSource for those specific cases.

Under the hood, JUnit runs the method body once per row of data, and each run shows up as its own entry in the report. I can customize that label with the name attribute so the report reads clearly.

The common mistakes are using the regular Test annotation by accident, in which case the parameters never get injected, and reaching for MethodSource when CsvSource would be simpler. The dependency is junit-jupiter-params, but Spring Boot's test starter already pulls it in. To stand out, I'd say the real win is removing duplication while making the boundary cases explicit and easy to read.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**`@Nested`** lets you put related tests inside an inner, non-static class so the report reads like an outline — e.g.

a `WhenAccountIsEmpty` group under `BankAccountTest`.

Each nested class can have its own `@BeforeEach`, and outer `@BeforeEach` methods run **before** the nested ones, so you build context incrementally. It groups scenarios for the same unit; use separate top-level classes for genuinely different units.

Mixing JUnit 4 imports (org.junit.Test) with JUnit 5, or marking the test method public/returning a value out of habit

sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB S["Argument source
@ValueSource / @CsvSource
/ @MethodSource"] --> R["JUnit runs the
method once per row"] R --> I1["invocation 1
args row 1"] R --> I2["invocation 2
args row 2"] R --> I3["invocation N
args row N"] ```

sections.title: Three Common Sources
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `@Test`.** A parameterized method needs `@ParameterizedTest`; with `@Test` the parameters won't be injected.
- **Wrong source for the data.** `@ValueSource` only carries one argument; for input/expected pairs use `@CsvSource`.
- **Forgetting the dependency.** Parameterized tests live in `junit-jupiter-params`, which `spring-boot-starter-test` already includes.
- **`@MethodSource` factory not static.** It must be `static` (unless using `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)`).

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: **JUnit 5** is a modular rewrite of **JUnit 4**. Annotations were renamed (`@Before`→`@BeforeEach`, `@BeforeClass`→`@BeforeAll`, `@Ignore`→`@Disabled`), exception testing moved to **`assertThrows`** (vs `@Test(expected=)`), the runner model `@RunWith` became the extension model **`@ExtendWith`**, it requires **Java 8+**, and it adds `@DisplayName`, `@Nested`, and first-class parameterized tests.

questions.question: How do you test that a method throws an exception in JUnit 5?
questions.title: Test Exception JUnit 5 Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: In JUnit 5 you test exceptions with **`assertThrows(ExpectedException.class, executable)`**, passing the call as a lambda. It **asserts the exception type was thrown and returns the exception object**, so you can then assert on its message or cause. This replaces JUnit 4's `@Test(expected = ...)`, which couldn't inspect the message or pinpoint which line threw.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you use assertThrows correctly and verify the message, not just the type
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using try/catch with fail(), or the JUnit 4 @Test(expected=) style which can't check the message
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Capture the returned exception and assert on getMessage()/getCause(); mention assertDoesNotThrow for the negative case

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`assertThrows(Type.class, lambda)`** — checks the type and returns the exception.
- **Inspect the message** — `ex.getMessage()` / `ex.getCause()` after capturing it.
- **Replaces `@Test(expected=)`** — which couldn't read the message.
- **`assertDoesNotThrow`** — for the negative case.
- **Keep the lambda minimal** — only the call that should throw.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
In JUnit 5 I test exceptions with assertThrows. I give it the exception class I expect and a lambda that wraps the call that should throw. If the code doesn't throw, or throws the wrong type, the test fails. The really useful part is that on success assertThrows returns the exception object, so I can then assert on its message or its cause.

That's a big improvement over the old JUnit 4 way, which was the Test annotation with expected equals the exception class. That style only checked the type — it couldn't look at the message, and it couldn't tell you which line in the method actually threw, so any statement throwing that type would make the test pass for the wrong reason.

So a good exception test does two things: it confirms the right type was thrown, and it checks the message is what I expect. For example, I'd capture the exception from assertThrows when I divide by zero, and then assertEquals that the message is divisor must not be zero. I keep the lambda small — only the call that should throw goes inside — so the assertion proves that specific line threw. There's also assertDoesNotThrow for the negative case, where I want to prove a valid input runs cleanly.

The mistakes I'd avoid are using try-catch with a fail call, which is verbose and easy to get wrong, and asserting on a broad superclass like Exception, which passes for almost anything. To stand out, I'd point out that assertThrows returning the exception lets me downcast to a custom exception and check its fields too.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**`@Nested`** lets you put related tests inside an inner, non-static class so the report reads like an outline — e.g.

a `WhenAccountIsEmpty` group under `BankAccountTest`.

Each nested class can have its own `@BeforeEach`, and outer `@BeforeEach` methods run **before** the nested ones, so you build context incrementally. It groups scenarios for the same unit; use separate top-level classes for genuinely different units.

Mixing JUnit 4 imports (org.junit.Test) with JUnit 5, or marking the test method public/returning a value out of habit

sections.title: JUnit 4 style: can't inspect the message
JUnit 5 assertThrows: precise and inspectable
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **try/catch + fail().** Verbose and easy to get wrong (a missing `fail()` makes the test pass when nothing throws). Use `assertThrows`.
- **Only checking the type.** Two bugs can throw the same exception type; assert the message too.
- **Wrapping too much in the lambda.** Put only the throwing call inside, so the assertion proves *that* line threw.
- **Asserting a superclass.** `assertThrows(Exception.class, ...)` passes for almost anything; assert the most specific type.

questions.direct_answer: **JUnit 5** is a modular rewrite of **JUnit 4**. Annotations were renamed (`@Before`→`@BeforeEach`, `@BeforeClass`→`@BeforeAll`, `@Ignore`→`@Disabled`), exception testing moved to **`assertThrows`** (vs `@Test(expected=)`), the runner model `@RunWith` became the extension model **`@ExtendWith`**, it requires **Java 8+**, and it adds `@DisplayName`, `@Nested`, and first-class parameterized tests.

sections.title: What Changed from JUnit 4 to 5
sections.content: **JUnit 5** (2017) is a ground-up redesign of **JUnit 4**. The headline difference is **architecture**: JUnit 4 was one jar with a single `@RunWith` runner; JUnit 5 splits into Platform, Jupiter, and Vintage, and replaces the single runner with composable **extensions** via `@ExtendWith`. The everyday differences are renamed annotations and better exception/parameterized support. JUnit 5 needs **Java 8+** for lambdas. Vintage lets old JUnit 4 tests keep running while you migrate.

sections.title: JUnit 4 vs 5 at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|JUnit 4|~Single jar + runner|@Before / @BeforeClass|@Test(expected=)|one @RunWith only
emerald|JUnit 5|~Modular, lambda-based|@BeforeEach / @BeforeAll|assertThrows(...)|many @ExtendWith
blue|Migration|~They can coexist|Vintage runs old tests|rename annotations|move runners to extensions

sections.title: Concrete API Mapping
sections.content:
| Concern | JUnit 4 | JUnit 5 |
|---|---|---|
| Test marker | `@Test` (`org.junit`) | `@Test` (`org.junit.jupiter.api`) |
| Before each | `@Before` | `@BeforeEach` |
| Once before | `@BeforeClass` | `@BeforeAll` (static) |
| Skip | `@Ignore` | `@Disabled("reason")` |
| Exceptions | `@Test(expected=X)` | `assertThrows(X.class, ...)` |
| Extend | `@RunWith(X.class)` | `@ExtendWith(X.class)` |
| Readable names | n/a | `@DisplayName` |
| Java version | Java 5+ | Java 8+ |

sections.title: JUnit 4 test
JUnit 5 equivalent
Migration Notes
sections.content: You don't have to rewrite everything at once. Add **JUnit Vintage** so existing JUnit 4 tests keep running on the JUnit 5 platform, then migrate class by class: swap imports to `org.junit.jupiter.api`, rename `@Before`→`@BeforeEach` and `@BeforeClass`→`@BeforeAll` (make it static), convert `@Test(expected=)` to `assertThrows`, and replace `@RunWith` with `@ExtendWith`. Avoid mixing JUnit 4 and 5 annotations in the *same* class — that's where the confusing failures come from.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Architecture** — JUnit 5 is modular (Platform/Jupiter/Vintage) vs JUnit 4's single jar.
- **Annotations renamed** — `@Before`→`@BeforeEach`, `@BeforeClass`→`@BeforeAll`, `@Ignore`→`@Disabled`.
- **Exceptions** — `assertThrows` replaces `@Test(expected=)` and can check the message.
- **Extensions** — `@ExtendWith` replaces `@RunWith` and can stack multiple.
- **Coexistence** — Vintage runs JUnit 4 tests during migration; don't mix in one class.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JUnit 5 is basically a ground-up rewrite of JUnit 4, and the differences fall into a few buckets. The biggest is architecture. JUnit 4 was a single jar with one runner mechanism, the RunWith annotation, and you could only have one runner per class. JUnit 5 is modular — it splits into the Platform that launches tests, the Jupiter API I write against, and Vintage that runs old JUnit 4 tests. And instead of a single runner, it uses extensions through the ExtendWith annotation, which you can stack, so I can combine, say, the Mockito extension and the Spring extension on the same class.

Then there are the renamed annotations, which is what trips up freshers. Before became BeforeEach, BeforeClass became BeforeAll and has to be static, and Ignore became Disabled, where I pass a reason. The imports also change — everything moves to org dot junit dot jupiter dot api.

Exception testing changed too. In JUnit 4 you wrote Test with expected equals the exception class, but that only checked the type and couldn't look at the message. In JUnit 5 I use assertThrows, which returns the exception so I can assert on its message. JUnit 5 also needs Java 8 or later because the API uses lambdas, and it adds nice things like DisplayName and Nested.

The practical mistake is mixing JUnit 4 and 5 annotations in the same class, which causes confusing behavior. To migrate, I add Vintage so old tests keep running, then convert class by class. To stand out, I'd highlight that ExtendWith replaced RunWith and lets you compose multiple extensions.

questions.question: How do you add JUnit 5 to a Maven project?
questions.title: Add JUnit 5 to Maven Project | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Add JUnit 5 to Maven with the **`junit-jupiter`** aggregator dependency in **`test`** scope, and make sure the **Maven Surefire** plugin is recent enough (3.x) to discover Jupiter tests. In a Spring Boot project you get all of this for free via **`spring-boot-starter-test`**, so you rarely add JUnit directly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can configure a build to run JUnit 5 tests and know Spring Boot bundles it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding only junit-jupiter-api (so tests compile but the engine is missing at runtime), or an old Surefire that ignores Jupiter
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that junit-jupiter pulls api + engine + params, and spring-boot-starter-test already includes JUnit 5, Mockito, and AssertJ

sections.title: Wiring JUnit 5 into a Maven Build
sections.content: Two things must be in place. First, the **dependency**: the convenient `junit-jupiter` aggregator pulls in the API (to compile tests), the engine (to run them), and params (for parameterized tests), all in **`test`** scope so it never ships to production. Second, the **Maven Surefire** plugin must be version **3.x or newer** to discover JUnit Platform tests during `mvn test`. In a **Spring Boot** project, `spring-boot-starter-test` already bundles JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, and Hamcrest — so you usually add nothing.

sections.title: What You Need at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Dependency|~junit-jupiter (test scope)|api to compile|engine to run|params for data tests
blue|Surefire plugin|~Runs unit tests|must be 3.x+|discovers JUnit Platform|else 0 tests run
amber|Spring Boot shortcut|~starter-test|bundles JUnit 5|Mockito + AssertJ|add nothing else
violet|Run|~mvn test / verify|Surefire = unit|Failsafe = integration|reports under target

sections.title: Steps to Add JUnit 5
sections.content:
| Step | What to do |
|---|---|
| 1 | Add `org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter` with `<scope>test</scope>` |
| 2 | Ensure `maven-surefire-plugin` is 3.x+ (auto in modern Spring Boot) |
| 3 | Put tests under `src/test/java`, class named `*Test` |
| 4 | Run `mvn test` (or `mvn verify`) |
| 5 | In Spring Boot, prefer `spring-boot-starter-test` and skip steps 1-2 |

sections.title: pom.xml Configuration
sections.content:
```xml
<!-- Plain Maven project -->
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>   <!-- api + engine + params -->
    <version>5.10.2</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.2.5</version>   <!-- 3.x discovers JUnit Platform tests -->
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
```
```xml
<!-- Spring Boot: this single starter already includes JUnit 5 -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only adding `junit-jupiter-api`.** Tests compile but fail to run because the engine isn't on the path. Use the `junit-jupiter` aggregator.
- **Old Surefire.** Surefire 2.x ignores JUnit Platform tests, so `mvn test` reports zero tests run.
- **Wrong scope.** Forgetting `<scope>test</scope>` leaks the test framework into the production jar.
- **Adding JUnit on top of Spring Boot.** Pulling a conflicting JUnit version can clash with the version the starter already manages.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`junit-jupiter`** aggregator = api + engine + params.
- **`test` scope** keeps it out of the production artifact.
- **Surefire 3.x+** is required to discover Jupiter tests.
- **`spring-boot-starter-test`** bundles JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ — add nothing extra.
- **Run** with `mvn test`; integration tests run on `mvn verify` via Failsafe.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
There are really two pieces to getting JUnit 5 running in Maven: the dependency and the plugin. For the dependency, the easiest thing is the junit-jupiter aggregator artifact, because it pulls in everything I need — the API so my tests compile, the engine so they actually run, and the params module for parameterized tests. I put it in test scope so it never ends up in the production jar.

The second piece is the Maven Surefire plugin, which is what runs unit tests during mvn test. It has to be version three or newer, because the older two-x line doesn't know how to discover JUnit Platform tests, and if you forget that, mvn test happily reports zero tests run, which is confusing.

Now, in practice, if I'm on a Spring Boot project I almost never do any of that, because spring-boot-starter-test already bundles JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, and Hamcrest, all in test scope, with compatible versions managed for me. So I just add that one starter and I'm done.

The mistakes I'd watch for are adding only the junit-jupiter-api artifact, which makes tests compile but not run because the engine is missing, using an old Surefire that silently ignores the tests, and forgetting the test scope. To stand out, I'd mention that the aggregator gives you api, engine, and params together, and that on Spring Boot the starter already covers the whole testing stack.

questions.question: What is @Nested in JUnit 5 and when would you use it?
questions.title: @Nested JUnit 5 Tests | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`@Nested`** lets you put related tests inside an inner, non-static class so the report reads like an outline — e.g. a `WhenAccountIsEmpty` group under `BankAccountTest`. Each nested class can have its own `@BeforeEach`, and outer `@BeforeEach` methods run **before** the nested ones, so you build context incrementally. It groups scenarios for the same unit; use separate top-level classes for genuinely different units.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can organize tests by scenario and understand nested @BeforeEach ordering
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Making the nested class static (which breaks @Nested), or expecting @BeforeAll inside a nested class without PER_CLASS
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that outer @BeforeEach runs before inner @BeforeEach, letting each layer add setup

sections.title: Grouping Tests by Scenario
sections.content: **`@Nested`** marks an **inner, non-static** class whose tests belong to a sub-scenario of the outer class. It turns a flat list of test methods into a readable tree: `BankAccountTest → WhenAccountIsEmpty → withdrawThrows`. Each nested class can declare its own `@BeforeEach` for scenario-specific setup, and JUnit runs the **outer** `@BeforeEach` first, then the inner one — so you layer context from general to specific. Use `@Nested` to group tests of the *same* unit by state or condition; use separate top-level classes for different units.

sections.title: @Nested at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|What it is|~Inner non-static class|groups by scenario|reads like an outline|same unit, many states
blue|Lifecycle|~Setup layers|outer @BeforeEach first|then inner @BeforeEach|build context step by step
amber|Gotchas|~Easy to misuse|must NOT be static|@BeforeAll needs PER_CLASS|don't over-nest (2 levels)
violet|When to use|~Organize big classes|group empty vs funded|happy vs error paths|clearer failure reports

sections.title: Nested Tests with Layered Setup
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Making the nested class `static`.** `@Nested` requires a non-static inner class so it can access the outer instance; `static` breaks it.
- **Expecting `@BeforeAll` inside a nested class.** It needs `@TestInstance(PER_CLASS)` because `@BeforeAll` is static by default.
- **Over-nesting.** Three or four levels deep hurts readability; two levels is usually plenty.
- **Using `@Nested` for unrelated units.** Different classes under test belong in different top-level test classes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Nested`** = inner non-static class grouping a sub-scenario.
- **Setup layers** — outer `@BeforeEach` runs before inner `@BeforeEach`.
- **Non-static required** — a `static` nested class won't be picked up.
- **Readable reports** — failures show as `Outer → Scenario → test`.
- **Same unit, many states** — split unrelated units into separate classes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Nested is an annotation I put on an inner, non-static class to group related tests together. Without it, a big test class is just a flat list of methods. With it, the report reads like an outline — for example, under BankAccountTest I might have a group called when the account is empty and another called when the account has a hundred, and the tests live inside those groups. That makes failures much easier to read because you see the scenario right there in the report.

The really useful part is the lifecycle. Each nested class can have its own BeforeEach, and JUnit runs the outer BeforeEach first and then the inner one. So in the bank account example, the outer BeforeEach creates a fresh account, and then inside the funded group, an inner BeforeEach deposits a hundred. That lets me layer the setup from general to specific instead of repeating it.

There are a couple of gotchas. The nested class must be non-static — if you make it static, JUnit won't treat it as a nested test class, because it needs access to the outer instance. And if you want a BeforeAll inside a nested class, you have to switch to the per-class test instance lifecycle, since BeforeAll is static by default. I'd also avoid nesting too deeply; two levels is usually plenty.

The rule of thumb is to use Nested to group tests of the same unit by state or condition — empty versus funded, happy path versus error path — and to use separate top-level classes for genuinely different units. To stand out, I'd mention that outer BeforeEach runs before inner BeforeEach, which is what makes the layered setup work.
